Capital requests from the DPW exceed what can likely be funded, so prioritising them before funding amounts are known shapes which road and equipment projects reach spring town meeting.
The bridge contract and the planned land transfers to conservation are items residents may be asked to weigh in on or vote on at town meeting.

A presentation on planned land transfers to conservation ahead of spring town meeting, as requested.

A long joint session on the skate park debated moving it from beside TC Passios to Marshall Park, and its size; no vote was taken.
The board and Parks Commission appointed Anna Lockwood as the fifth Parks Commission member; the vote was stated as seven to zero with one abstention.
The board approved the Salvation Army boot drive request for Dec 12 by roll call.
The board nominated Michael Ray Jeffries as its MART appointee, and a meeting on the old primary school was targeted for January 12.

why_it_matters: License fees stay as they are, so local businesses hurt by COVID get no fee cut from the town. The fees are built into local receipts in the budget, and the town manager's help with recovery funds is the route offered instead.
The skate park's site and size are still open. Moving it to Marshall Park would change which park land and which project costs residents are asked to support.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted 4-0 by roll call to accept the BrightFarms TIF agreement (draft seven) and recommend the article to Special Town Meeting.
The vote commits the board to recommend the TIF article at the special town meeting the next evening.
The agreement ends at eight years or when the maximum exemption, defined as a dollar cap, is reached, whichever comes first.
BrightFarms pays full taxes on improvements as assessed until occupancy and completion; the TIF engages only at completion.
The job commitment in the agreement can fall to a floor and no lower.

why_it_matters: A TIF exempts part of a company's added property value from tax for a set period, so the cap and the eight-year limit set how much tax the town gives up on this project.
Town Meeting voters, not the board, decide whether the article passes, and the job floor and the full taxes during construction are the terms they can weigh.

why_it_matters: A single tax rate means homes and businesses are taxed at the same rate per thousand dollars of value, rather than shifting more of the levy onto commercial and industrial property.

The 360 Flat Hill Road decision keeps the town's option to buy the land open while the open space committee reports, and the BrightFarms TIF would set the tax break the company receives on its property.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted 5-0 to recommend several Special Town Meeting articles, including the street light conversion, the capital plan and the sewer reserve deposit.
The board took up the ratification of Thomas Gamel as police chief; the minutes record the vote outcome as not audible.
The board ratified the assessing assistant appointment 5-0 and adopted the signage on town property policy 5-0.
Several articles were left without a recommendation, and the board named an eight-year schedule as its lead option for the Bright Farms TIF.
The board set a members-only site walk of the old primary school site for Oct 31 and an open meeting law complaint led to a heated exchange.

why_it_matters: The recommended articles, especially the street light purchase and how it fixes the stabilization amount, are items residents will be asked to vote on at Special Town Meeting and can affect the tax bill.
The Bright Farms TIF schedule and the old primary school site decisions bear on future tax revenue and on how a town-owned property is used.
watch_next: Nov 3: the board is to choose a date (Dec 1 or Dec 14) for the skateboard park tri-party meeting.
Finance Committee meeting on the 29th, to which the board was invited, and the Special Town Meeting articles still deferred.

what_happened.line: The Select Board directed that a Bright Farms tax increment financing deal proceed on an eight-year term, kept revenue neutral if possible, with a ten-year version as an alternative.
The board decided the right of first refusal at 250 Howard Street is not waived until a tri-party agreement, drafted by town counsel and the town manager, is in place.
The board granted a wine and malt package store license to Lanni Orchards, 5-0 by roll call.
The board told the town manager to proceed with selling a small town-owned piece at 671 West Street and to notify only the two abutters.
The board approved a bond anticipation note renewal and signed the November 3, 2020 election warrant, both by roll call.

why_it_matters: A tax increment financing deal discounts a company's property taxes for a set number of years, so its term and revenue-neutral condition decide how much new tax revenue the town gives up or collects.

The 250 Howard Street agreement and the 671 West Street sale both affect whether town-held land is protected as open space or passes into private hands, and the Howard Street question may come to residents as a warrant article.

meetings.summary: The board heard the Open Space Committee chair explain why the town should consider buying a Chapter 61 parcel at 250 Howard Street, and heard from the prospective buyers. The prospective buyers were asked to work with the Open Space Committee before the warrant closes for the Sept 29 special town meeting.

why_it_matters: If the town buys the 250 Howard Street parcel, the cost would come from the town budget, mostly taxes, and a special town meeting vote would likely be needed to approve it.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted 3-2 to pay the two school bus companies the amounts the school committee approved for the spring school closure.
A motion not to support any payment to the bus companies failed for lack of a second before the 3-2 roll call vote.
The board authorized the town manager to post two new Parks Commission vacancies for joint appointment until the next annual election.
The board accepted the special town meeting timeline, with the warrant opening Wednesday September 2, and tabled the FY2021 budget discussion to next week.
The board voted 5-0 not to recommend naming a tributary after a non-resident, and will send that response to the federal naming board.

why_it_matters: The bus payments for months when schools were closed come from the town budget, mostly taxes, and the 3-2 split shows the board divided over paying private contractors for service not delivered.
The special town meeting, where residents will vote on articles, and the FY2021 budget discussion are both still unsettled, as are the safety arrangements for attending in person.
watch_next: Next week: the finance director's fourth quarter report, the FY2021 budget discussion and the special town meeting articles, plus a revised meeting safety plan.
Parks Commission interviews later in the month for the two interim seats.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted 4-1 to designate a dog dangerous after a bite at a private beach, ending a continued hearing.
The board then voted 5-0 to order a muzzle and restraint off premises, proof of insurance, and identification information for the dog.
Town counsel is to draft a written determination for board review; the owner then has 10 days to appeal.
The board voted 5-0 to accept a letter asking MassDOT for a nighttime heavy-vehicle restriction on four town roads.
The board amended its remote participation policy to add caring for an ill person as a permissible reason, and appointed a personnel committee member.

why_it_matters: The dog orders set the legal conditions the owner must meet, and the written determination starts the appeal period.
The truck letter is only a request to the state; any restriction depends on MassDOT, and a civil fine for violating a truck exclusion sign was described as small.
A tri-centennial committee could bring a funding request to a future Town Meeting vote.
watch_next: Ms. Adams' draft concept and motion wording for a tri-centennial committee, due at next week's meeting.
The written determination from town counsel on the dangerous dog, and the owner's 10-day appeal window after service.

what_happened.line: The dangerous dog hearing was continued to August 11 by roll call vote, all aye, because the complainant and a witness were absent.
The board raised the FY21 town counsel monthly retainer by roll call vote; counsel cited inflation since 2017 and the town manager said the legal account can cover it.
The board amended a flammable storage license to add a diesel tank at the Gulf station on Mass Ave, and approved a stop sign on Goodridge Street at Reservoir Road.
The board ratified an interim police lieutenant, with one abstention, and appointed members to the personnel and agricultural commissions.
The board adopted its FY21 goals and the town manager's goals, and approved the Central Mass Regional Stormwater Coalition agreement.

why_it_matters: The higher town counsel retainer is a recurring legal cost paid from the town budget, mostly taxes, and the board was told existing funds cover it for FY21.
The diesel tank approval and the dog hearing touch neighborhood safety and licensing, and the dog hearing will be heard again with the complainant's testimony still to come.
State aid held at no less than the FY20 level as a baseline, which bears on how much of FY21 must be raised locally.
watch_next: August 11: the continued dangerous dog hearing, with written or live testimony sought from the complainant and a witness.
August 18: earth removal permit renewals, with board members sending written questions to the building commissioner beforehand.

why_it_matters: The streetlight purchase would draw on free cash, and members discussed whether that reduces the free cash available for the stabilization deposit, so the outcome touches the town's reserves and future tax pressure.

The town manager's answer on the funding source for Green Communities grants, due before Thursday.

what_happened.line: The Select Board awarded the bid for the 17 and 23 West Street properties on a 3-1 vote, after a member said the price seemed too low against appraised value.
The board reviewed the June 13 town meeting COVID safety plan and agreed to amend it on seating and masks, with the revised plan going out by email review without a board vote.
The board approved, 4-0 by roll call, the town manager's request to submit CARES Act reimbursement requests, with the first FY20 submission due June 5.
The board approved, 4-0 by roll call, a letter of support for a regional CDBG application covering micro-enterprise help and food assistance.
The board approved the 994 Northfield Road conservation restriction 4-0, contingent on the access easement and subordination agreement being executed.

why_it_matters: The West Street sale sets what the town receives for two town-owned properties, and the town manager said the RFP process may deter bidders compared with a regular listing.

CARES Act reimbursement and the regional grant are outside funds that can offset COVID costs and support local small businesses and food assistance, and the safety plan shapes how residents attend and vote at the June 13 town meeting.
watch_next: The revised town meeting safety plan, to be sent to the public for email review before the June 13 annual town meeting.
Outdoor restaurant seating guidance on next week's agenda, with four restaurants meeting the board June 9, and a proposed MVP listening session on June 16.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted to proceed with the Saliba property purchase at 994 Northfield Road and authorized the chair to sign the documents.
The Board first declared the Saliba purchase a unique acquisition, with all four members voting aye.
Most of the meeting went to safety precautions for an in-person June Town Meeting; a working group will draft a plan and Town Meeting was not postponed.
Members disagreed over the FY2021 budget, a free cash change, a possible state aid cut, and hiring a principal assessor during a hiring freeze.
The Board voted 4-0 by roll call to move the skateboard park tollbooth request to September 26, 2020.

why_it_matters: The Saliba purchase commits state grant money and town funds approved at an earlier special town meeting to a land acquisition.
How Town Meeting is held, and whether the FY2021 budget rests on state aid and free cash that may shrink, shapes how and when residents can vote on the budget that sets next year's tax bill.
watch_next: June 2 Select Board meeting: the town manager's draft Town Meeting plan, the West Street bid award, and write-in candidate outreach are due on the agenda.
Board members are to email the town clerk for her election plan.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted 4-0 on roll call to adopt the bond vote for the final borrowing for pavement management and the middle/high school project.
The board recommended the capital plan as presented (3-1, one abstention) and recommended the FY2021 budget as presented, with one member opposed.
The board removed the old primary school article from the warrant 3-2, and later removed the Community Preservation Act article.
The board deferred the streetlight purchase, the sewer enterprise fund, earth removal changes and liquor license petition articles to Town Meeting.
The board signed the annual Town Meeting and election warrant, and asked that Town Meeting pandemic planning go on next week's agenda.

why_it_matters: The capital plan is funded fully by free cash, so the recommended projects and the streetlight purchase compete for the same unappropriated money rather than new taxes, and residents will vote on them at Town Meeting.
Articles that were deferred have no board recommendation yet, and the removed old primary school and Community Preservation articles will not be on the Town Meeting warrant.
watch_next: Next week's Select Board agenda: planning for holding Town Meeting safely during the pandemic, and the pledge of allegiance.
Board recommendations at Town Meeting on the deferred articles, including streetlights and earth removal article BB after its presentation.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted 4-0 to recommend a consensus list of annual town meeting warrant articles, after removing the collective bargaining, OPEB and PAC capital articles.
The board voted 4-0 to approve an all-alcohol restaurant license transfer with a pledge, and 4-0 to return a pizzeria license to its prior owner.
The board heard the DPW director, the chiefs and the Conservation Commission on where to site the town fuel tanks near Mopus Brook; no action was taken.
On a citizen petition for an additional liquor license, the board will ask town counsel whether the wording can be amended on the floor before voting to support it.
Held articles move to the May 12 meeting; the town manager evaluation was postponed until after the election.

why_it_matters: The recommended warrant articles are what residents will be asked to vote on at town meeting, and the deferred OPEB article and the FY21 budget adjustments bear on future tax bills.
The fuel tank location is undecided, so the cost and siting of a town facility near a brook remain open.
watch_next: May 12 Select Board meeting, which is to cover the remaining warrant articles.
Town counsel's answer on whether the citizen petition wording can be amended on the floor.

The state senator and representative told the joint meeting that state aid and the state budget are not settled and declined to give a cut percentage.
The Town Manager presented a revised FY21 budget with new positions cut, a smaller school increase, a halved capital plan and a surplus held as a cushion.
The Community Preservation Act article was held to next week's agenda so the vote can be taken with a fuller board.
Members debated a warrant article moving free cash into the OPEB stabilization fund, and one member wants it removed.

why_it_matters: The FY21 budget that Town Meeting will be asked to approve rests on state aid figures that were still unknown, so the tax impact and any later cuts could change.

what_happened.line: Three members said they would not support the Community Preservation Act on the warrant now; the proponent has a week to consult her group before a vote.
Members debated how conservative the town manager's FY21 budget is, including state aid and new growth assumptions; nothing was resolved and it continues next week.
The board voted 3-0 to approve a bicycle charity ride, conditioned on the governor's emergency order being lifted and public health conditions allowing.
The DPW fuel tank location will go on a future agenda with stakeholders invited, though not next week; the town manager said a state earmark means no June 30 deadline.
A resident asked for late fees and interest on tax bills to be waived; the town manager said the board had waived them through June 29.

why_it_matters: The Community Preservation Act would add a surcharge to property tax bills if it reaches the June town meeting ballot, and the board's vote next week decides whether the article stays on the warrant.
The budget debate turns on how much cushion the tax levy keeps if state aid or local receipts fall short, which affects the size of next year's tax bill and the services it pays for.
The fuel tank siting touches a riverfront area near homes, and residents will have a chance to weigh in when it is scheduled.
watch_next: Next week's Select Board meeting: vote on keeping the CPA article on the warrant, then budget first, warrant articles, and a joint session with legislators.
Members seeking budget cuts are asked to bring specific lists to next week's meeting.

The town manager reported that the FY21 budget outlook is uncertain, and members pressed for more conservative planning.

what_happened.line: The Select Board approved emergency COVID-19 measures: a paid sick leave policy, a Family Medical Leave policy, and a request to the state for emergency spending approval.
The board kept the May 1 tax due date but extended the exemption deadline and waived penalties and interest to June 29.
The board granted a wine and malt license to Smokestack Roasters and an all-alcohol license plus entertainment licenses to Whiskey Girl Bar; one member voted no on the all-alcohol license.
The board voted 4-0-1 not to exercise the town's right of first refusal on Chapter 61 land at Holman Street and Northfield Road.
The Community Preservation Act ballot question was deferred a week, and the town manager described an FY21 budget shortfall even after cuts.

why_it_matters: The tax penalty waiver and the leave policies bear directly on household bills and on workers' pay during the pandemic.
The town manager described an FY21 budget that remains short even with new positions removed and state aid held level, so service levels and next year's tax bill are uncertain.
A Community Preservation Act ballot question would add a surcharge to property tax bills if voters approve it. It is still undecided.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted to put a streetlight article on the Town Meeting warrant, subject to town counsel, after hearing a recommendation to buy the lights from Unitil.
The board voted 3-2 to place the four Chapter 61 properties on the annual Town Meeting warrant as placeholders pending reports from land-use bodies.
The board announced that an article to purchase 635 Mass Ave will be added to the warrant after the executive session.
The board approved a skate park tollbooth fundraiser on June 6, a common victualer license for Al Forno, and two Agricultural Commission appointments.
A joint meeting with the Planning Board was set for March 23, and a workshop on the old primary school was set for the 31st.

why_it_matters: The streetlight article could change what the town pays each year for street lighting and maintenance, and Town Meeting voters will be asked to decide whether the town buys the lights.
The Chapter 61 placeholders and the 635 Mass Ave article put land-purchase and right-of-first-refusal questions on the Town Meeting warrant, which residents will be asked to vote on.
watch_next: Joint meeting of the Select Board and Planning Board on March 23 at 7:30, with master planning added to the agenda.
The town manager's performance review procedure, due on next week's Select Board agenda.

what_happened.line: The Select Board held a public session on the five-year forecast and the FY2021 capital plan and took no budget vote.
Residents questioned whether the school staffing plan is affordable, and one said the forecast shows a shortfall in year five.
The superintendent explained the staffing needs behind the school budget increase, and a member asked how to reach a lower increase.
Capital items for the public safety carport, the Ritter building kitchen and ramp, and TC Passios were questioned; no capital money is allocated for TC Passios needs.
The board went into executive session on collective bargaining after noting future agenda items and upcoming meeting dates.

why_it_matters: The school budget increase and the capital plan both feed the town budget, mostly taxes, so the questions raised here bear on what tax bills could carry in FY2021.
Spending on the Ritter building and TC Passios is unsettled while the town has not decided what to do with its buildings, and no capital money is allocated to the needs identified at TC Passios.
watch_next: The town manager is to present the budget to the Finance Committee on the 13th.
Interviews of three design firms for TC Passios were announced for the next day at 6 pm.

meetings.headline: Board approved an earth removal permit 3-2 with conditions; denied firearm hunting on conservation land 3-2.
meetings.summary: The Select Board denied a request to hunt with firearms on town conservation land, licensed a new auto dealer, and, after a long hearing with abutters objecting, approved a 50,000 cubic yard earth removal permit with conditions. The town manager presented the FY21-25 five-year financial forecast and the FY21 capital plan, and the superintendent discussed the school staffing plan, which drew sharp objections from one member. Routine appointments, a power broker agreement and a charter letter were also handled.

meetings.headline: Select Board backed demolishing the old primary school for a town green and voted to pursue assessments and a spring article.
meetings.summary: The board held a workshop on the old primary school building and land, reviewing ranked-choice results of the informal town poll that favored a town green. Members debated the Architectural Preservation District's power over demolition and how to fund assessments. Two motions were taken by voice vote, and the town manager was asked to report on funding next meeting. Routine items covered DPW vacancies, a Complete Streets grant, and Brownfields funding for 925 Mass Ave.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted to open the annual Town Meeting warrant on January 14th and close it on March 16th at 4 p.m.; the outcome was not captioned.
The town manager said she would get an estimate for a hazardous-materials assessment of the old primary building, which the town owns.
A member suggested paying for the assessment now rather than waiting for the fiscal 21 budget; the cost was uncertain.
The board was told of additional Chapter 90 road money for the town's fiscal 20 apportionment.
A resident said the Charter approved at May Town Meeting has not been certified, which could keep added Parks Commission seats from being filled in May.

why_it_matters: The old primary school is town property, and the assessment estimate will show whether its hazard cleanup is paid from this year's funds or waits for the fiscal 21 budget and a Town Meeting vote.
The warrant lists the articles voters will decide at Town Meeting, so the open window from January 14th to March 16th is when items can be added.
If the Charter is not certified in time, new Parks Commission seats may not appear on the May ballot.
watch_next: The town manager's cost estimate for the old primary hazardous-materials assessment.
The warrant closes March 16th at 4 p.m.; a public budget-questions meeting is set for the 28th.
